title: Not ashamed (Romans 1:1–17)
hook: Paul introduces himself to a church he's never met, and to the good news as power

segments.voice: Yesterday, life everlasting, and Julian's all shall be well, the end of the creed. Your line was mercy has the last word. Who did you leave to mercy? Day three hundred twelve.

Think about writing to someone you've never met, but hope to. A new team you're about to join. A family you're marrying into. You want them to know who you are, and you want them to like you, but you also have something important to say. How do you start? Around the year 57, Paul is in Corinth, in Greece, and he writes the longest letter we have from him, to the Christians in Rome. He's never been there. He didn't found that church. He's heard about them, and they've heard about him, perhaps not all of it good. And this letter would go on to change history more than once. Augustine, Luther and Wesley were all turned around by it. Today we begin a new part of the path: Romans. And its first big claim is today's word.
screen: `A LETTER TO STRANGERS.` → `CORINTH TO ROME, AROUND 57.` → `A LETTER THAT CHANGED HISTORY.`

segments.voice: Paul opens by telling them who he is: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, separated unto the gospel of God." Servant. The Greek word is doulos, a slave, someone who belongs to another. That's how he chooses to introduce himself. Then he greets them warmly: "To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints: Grace to you and peace." Remember saints from day three hundred seven: ordinary people, set apart. Then he says he longs to visit, so that he can give them some spiritual gift. And then he catches himself, and adds, in effect: I mean, so that we can encourage each other. "that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me." The great apostle, correcting himself mid-sentence, so he doesn't sound like he's coming to lecture them. Then comes the line the whole letter stands on: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek." Why would anyone be ashamed? Because in Rome, a crucified man was the lowest thing imaginable. The cross was the empire's punishment for slaves and rebels. And Paul says: I'm not ashamed of it. It's power. The Greek word is dynamis, where we get dynamic, and, much later, the word dynamite. Then one more line, quoted from the prophet Habakkuk, the line that would set Luther free fifteen centuries later: "The just shall live by faith."
screen: `DOULOS: A SERVANT WHO BELONGS.` · `TO ALL IN ROME, CALLED TO BE SAINTS.` · `SO WE CAN ENCOURAGE EACH OTHER.` · `THE CROSS AS POWER: DYNAMIS.` · then, large: `FOR I AM NOT ASHAMED OF THE GOSPEL OF CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare to introduce yourself kindly to someone new. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you don't know yet: a new neighbor, a new coworker, the person you always see and never speak to. Picture yourself saying hello. Notice Paul's way: say who you are, simply; greet them warmly; and let it be mutual, not you giving and them receiving, but two people encouraging each other. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name, or by face. If you don't, just picture the hello, and let it be warm. The bell holds the time.
Not ashamed. Paul's first big claim in Romans: he's not ashamed of the good news of a crucified Christ, because it is the power of God.
Your line: not ashamed. Today, introduce yourself kindly to someone new, and don't be ashamed of who you are. Day three hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Christians read Romans in church and in Bible studies, and many memorize Romans 1:16, "I am not ashamed of the gospel," as a statement of confidence in their faith.

original.note: Greek: power, ability. Paul's word in Romans 1:16; the root of dynamic, and much later of dynamite.

trapdoor: what you thought: not ashamed means being bold about your opinions.
what it means: Paul, writing to strangers in Rome, says he isn't ashamed of a crucified Christ, because the good news is God's power.
what a scholar hears: crucifixion was Rome's most shameful death, and Paul calls its message dynamis. Nobel named dynamite from the same Greek root.

notes: Romans dated c. 56–58, written from Corinth; script says 'around the year 57'. Confirm.
'Longest letter we have from him': Romans is the longest Pauline letter by word count. Confirm.
'Not all of it good' (rumors about Paul reaching Rome) inferred from Romans 3:8. Confirm phrasing.
Augustine (Romans 13:13–14, 386), Luther (Romans 1:17) and Wesley (Luther's preface to Romans, 1738): standard claims.
Nobel named dynamite from Greek dynamis (1867). Confirm.
Romans 1:7 KJV continues 'Grace to you and peace from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ'; quoted in part.
Romans 1:12 KJV opens 'That is, that I may be comforted...'; quoted from 'that I may'. 'Not all of it good' softened to 'perhaps not all of it good'.
